The properties of the particles resemble a special type of super-statistics for high values of the matrix $	heta_{\mu
u}$. The properties of the particles resemble a special type of super-statistics for high values of the matrix $	heta_{\mu
u}$.

We apply the two-photon absorption transient current technique to study the
properties of synthetic single-crystalline diamond. The first report on this
technique's application to diamond reveals its capacity to track charge transport
in three dimensions with high spatial resolution. The 2PH-TIC technique has been
used to study n-type and p-type dopants, exhibiting different energy-dependent
charge collection efficiencies that reflect the presence of synthetic diamond's
intrinsic defects. The technique's high spatial resolution enables the
determination of the thickness of the diamond's bulk and depletion region.

Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the prevalence of hate speech and offensive content. The various forms of hate speech identified in online discussions include gender-based violence, bullying, stigma, discrimination, and racism. A key challenge lies in the subjective interpretation of these categories, making the accurate classification of online content difficult. The complexity is further exacerbated by slang usage, neologisms, jargon, and the adaptation of English words in non-English speaking communities. To address these challenges, this research introduces a set of advanced natural language processing tasks aimed at extracting online content, labeling its genre, and assessing its level of hostility. These models demonstrate high levels of accuracy in identifying and categorizing hate speech, achieving a maximum accuracy of 83.51% in one task and 79.95% in another. The performance of these models outperforms existing benchmark results, making them valuable tools for developing automated content moderation systems on social media platforms.

This study centres around the solvability of a distinct class of fractional backward stochastic differential equations that take into account past influences within their generators, under Lipschitz condition it's demonstrated that the existence and uniqueness of such equations are assured. Furthermore, a key comparison theorem has been formulated.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's dynamics has a beneficial effect on policy updates and results in more resilient controllers. In addition, our findings highlight the practical advantages of this approach in a simulation-based evaluation.

Several key network communication challenges, such as caching and distributed computation, are increasingly important areas of study. A network caching scheme stores precomputed data in network caches to network files, using a coded caching scheme that leverages the principles of modern error correction codes. A distributed computation scheme, known as the Aggregation of Computation, uses coded computation to reduce communication costs in network computation, employing a distributed computation scheme that utilizes network computation resources and allows each network node to contribute to a target computation. Our proposed framework integrates both the principles of caching and computation into a unified theory, combining the networks, files, caches, network computation nodes, and input data vectors into a comprehensive framework. This framework demonstrates how a target data vector can be retrieved from a network cache, with the aid of a network computation server, using a combination of cache and computation requests, resulting in decreased network traffic. Our framework generalizes and encompasses the weighted file caching scheme, the equation sharing scheme, and the secure equation sharing scheme, as well as a new approach that combines cache and computation requests, termed the hybrid scheme. A traffic analysis of various schemes is presented, including a hybrid scheme that offers the most efficient solution. Furthermore, a distributed caching and computation scheme is proposed, combining cache and computation requests to further minimize network traffic costs.

We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for univalent type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad provides a viable way to handle partiality within univalent type theory, and we also demonstrate that a predicative and constructive Scott model is achievable. Notably, we avoid reliance on choice or quotient inductive-inductive types, unlike other approaches to dealing with partiality.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$.

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots, particularly those equipped with articulated arms, poses a significant challenge, especially when these robots operate in environments with inherent mobility uncertainties. To address this issue, this paper presents a novel nonlinear control approach that leverages the control barrier function framework, taking into account configuration-awareness and environmental safety. This approach integrates relative configuration information to enhance the dynamic flow field, resulting in more efficient path planning. Simulation and experimental results demonstrate the proposed method's ability to improve planning quality and secure navigation during operation.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity.

Researchers have been exploring the application of quantum computing using Bose-Einstein condensates, focusing on the role of its atom number. This study focuses on creating complex, single-beam quantum gates, such as the T gate, by implementing specific sequences of operations that leverage Kramers cranking, resonance acceleration, and a Raman pulse, followed by measurement-based feedback. It has been demonstrated through both analytical methods, applying perturbation theory, and numerical simulations, that these quantum gates function effectively when the condensate is in its fundamental state, but become inefficient when higher-order states are present. Specifically, it has been shown that a conditional phase shift is applied based on the atom number, but feedback is required to correct the shift and make the gate's action independent of the condensate's initial state. This study proposes an experimental protocol for implementing the T gate, but achieving it will necessitate further investigation into the behavior of BEC through advanced state preparation and the application of feedback.

This paper aims to accomplish two distinct objectives. Firstly, it seeks to establish a unicity theorem for meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a complex projective space, under the constraint of limited intersection with hypersurfaces. Secondly, the paper aims to prove a unicity theorem for the case of nondegenerate meromorphic mappings that share a specified number of hyperplanes in a particular geometric configuration.

Polynomial system solving has numerous applications in various fields, and to solve a system of polynomials, it's often necessary to first find its nondegenerate locus. Although the nondegenerate locus can't be represented as an algebraic set, specific representations can be computed to facilitate parameterization and dimension calculation. This paper presents a new algorithm that utilizes signature information to compute the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system in a progressive manner. Unlike existing methods, this algorithm's effectiveness doesn't rely on the degree of the polynomial system or the number of variables, but rather on the system's polynomial size. Furthermore, a crucial contribution is the development of an effective technique to compute a elimination ideal for an ideal with a Groebner basis in the degree-reversed lex order, using a progressive method.

Direct photons in Cu$+$Cu collisions at 200 GeV were measured using the PHENIX detector, covering all low-momentum ranges up to a maximum of 2.5 GeV/$c$ for transverse momentum and $|t|$ values of rapidity. After accounting for background and converting to per event and cross section, new data was obtained. Results show an increase in photon yield compared to nucleon $-$ nucleon collisions at lower momentum ranges and no significant change at higher values, consistent with earlier findings. An analysis was also carried out to compare these results with lead $-$ lead collisions at a higher energy of 62 GeV, where the ratio of photons to hadrons in lead $-$ lead collisions is known. An interesting observation was made with regard to the ratio of photons in copper $+$ copper and lead $-$ lead collisions, where the ratio deviates from one and an analysis was carried out to explain this difference, considering factors such as particle production and quark flavors.

The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new method for determining hypergraph extremality and apply it to derive a precise upper bound for the tetrahedron's extremal codegree sum. Our novel technique also allows us to calculate the asymptotic extremal codegree sum for the complete 4-vertex hypergraph K4.

Vector maps are widely used in modern society, appearing in applications such as navigation systems, in-store navigation, shop floor planning, and public signages. Since line joins are a fundamental element of vector maps, improving their quality is a significant area of research focus. Traditional anti-aliasing techniques, designed for raster images, degrade the sharpness of line caps and joins. A novel method, specifically tailored for line joins, uses a custom-rendering technique and an iterative algorithm to efficiently and accurately reconstruct them. The proposed technique has gained substantial attention in fields such as mobile rendering and visual analytics, showcasing its significant contributions and high-quality results.

The multivariate interpolation problem is often challenging to solve due to complex functions. This can result in difficult-to-handle large linear systems, and in some cases, the condition number may prevent any solution from being found at all. To address this issue, we propose a new rational interpolation scheme based on the transcendental RBF $(x^2+c)^{1/4}$. Our method involves calculating values at specific points rather than determining a complete function, which offers a more efficient and stable approach. We demonstrate its effectiveness with two new formulas for approximating functions, one for preserving the shape and another providing high-order accuracy, both of which surpass previously established methods in terms of accuracy.

Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emissions that originate from the
pulsar wind nebula's interaction with interstellar particles. Their properties,
such as spatial distribution, spectral characteristics, and polarization, provide
vital information about the underlying physical processes and the galaxy's
environment. Understanding pulsar halos contributes to the analysis of unidentified
multi-wavelength sources. This review summarizes the current state of research
on pulsar halos, including both observational findings and theoretical studies.

Visual weather classification is a multifaceted task involving the identification of four distinct weather conditions - sun, rain, fog, and snow - which are frequently encountered in driving scenarios. Accurate classification of these conditions is essential for drivers to make informed decisions and for autonomous vehicles to navigate safely. Current approaches often rely on convolutional neural networks, yet their performance gains have plateaued, and there is a lack of standardized evaluation protocols in the field. This research addresses these gaps by presenting a comprehensive evaluation of various convolutional neural models, introducing an efficient data augmentation technique, and releasing an extensive, diverse dataset comprising high-resolution images of each weather condition, which can be utilized to benchmark existing methods or train models for weather classification.

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later.

Soft grippers, thanks to their flexibility and resilience to damage, are ideal for multi-object grasping and the handling of fragile or irregularly shaped items. However, accurately controlling them to replicate a desired shape is complicated due to their nonlinear dynamics and the interplay of multiple physical forces. This research introduces a novel, data-driven approach to modeling and controlling a novel type of soft multi-fingered gripper utilizing the Online Measurement of a Covariant Online Koopman Operator (OMKO). The measurement can be taken without understanding the underlying physics, and sequential models generated from the measurements via regression allow for control via predictive state sequence optimization. The online nature of the models enables real-time updates as new data becomes available, and our developed system successfully achieves stable grasps of diverse objects and attains a desired control sequence.

One of the primary objectives in deep learning research is to bridge the gap between current model capabilities and their theoretical potential. Achieving this goal involves adapting Gradient Descent (GD), the primary optimization method in deep learning, which often struggles to converge efficiently due to its linear relationship with previous iterations. Research has developed a framework that generates an iterative approximation of GD, known as Fixed Point Method (FPM), which fits well with the structure of deep learning models and their non-differentiable optimization problems. However, GD corresponds to steepest descent using the Euclidean norm, whereas many deep learning objectives, especially those involving probability distributions, are better represented using divergences like KL or Wasserstein metrics rather than simple loss functions. In such cases, the Euclidean norm is less applicable, and the use of Natural Gradient Descent (NGD) is more suitable. Our work extends the FPM framework to Generalized FPM (GFPM), which facilitates smooth iteration of any differentiable function, and further generalizes it to Generalized Natural Gradient Descent (GNGD), which Generalized FPM mimics to a first-order accuracy. Our findings show that GNGD and GFPM converge to critical points under weakly-convex or bilinear assumptions and weakly-convex assumptions, respectively, and that GFPM fits well with the structural complexities of deep learning models, as evidenced by the successful application of its concepts, including a new metric for evaluating deep learning objectives' smoothness

High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide a direct look into the black hole's activity in the distant past. This is especially true for emissions in the radio to X-ray part of the spectrum, which can be linked directly to the black hole. A particularly significant finding in this area occurred on April 14, 2018, when a new radio source at the distance of z = 4.575 was discovered. This source, which has a location that matches a known active black hole, is the most distant object we know that emits radio waves in the range of a magnetosphere around a black hole. Observations of this object, which used a large radio telescope and took place a year and a half after its discovery, showed that it emits radio waves with powers of 4.5 and 4.9 milliwatts, which peak at a frequency of 9.3 GHz. The powers which it emits are similar to those which are predicted to result from a type of magnetosphere around the black hole. This is the first time that such a prediction has been confirmed in practice. The object, which emits a peak luminosity that is lower than a typical peak luminosity, may have a type of jet that is not pointing directly at the observer. Information about the object, which includes its peak luminosity, its distance, and the mass of the black hole, can be used to estimate either a peak luminosity that is higher than

This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in previous studies, still falls short of fully addressing the problem. Existing methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, struggle to effectively incorporate a wide range of clinical factors, making it challenging to break down the influence of different data types on model performance. To address this, we developed a novel network architecture that integrates text and image modalities to learn the impact of clinical factors and use it to enhance prognosis. We conducted a comprehensive study on a cohort of 1,451 patients, comparing our method to more than ten state-of-the-art approaches and discovering that our method outperforms the others in predicting overall survival time, with a C-index of 0.643 and 0.704 for two specific patient groups.

A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies.

A new method combining machine learning is proposed, enabling the reconstruction of high-resolution quasar absorption spectra. This approach utilizes neural networks to generate realistic synthetic spectra from simulations. The reconstructed power spectra achieved via this method surpass the accuracy of traditional approaches. The proposed reconstruction algorithm's complexity is neutral, facilitating potential application to large datasets, such as those from upcoming surveys. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through the analysis of simulated datasets of quasar spectra.

This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type, specifically those related to the Lie algebras of differential operators on a line. These modules are meant to be free over the U-algebras (denoted $U(\frak h)$) that are subalgebras (specifically parabolic subalgebras) of the universal enveloping algebras (den $U(\frak g)$) of the Lie algebras (den $\frak g$) that are also the Lie algebras of vector fields on a line. It is proven that the modules we've found are truly free over the $U(\frak h)$ algebras, but are not modules that are truly *cyclic* over that U-algebras. Additionally, this paper establishes the isomorphism between the space of U($\frak h$)-module maps from $M_{\lambda}$ to $M_{\mu}$ with itself, which is equivalent to the field of rational numbers.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue systems have led to a significant shift in focus towards large-scale language models. Although these models provide substantial improvements in generating natural and coherent responses, they often fail to meet specific requirements from a single user, such as those defined by their characteristics and preferences. To address this challenge, we aim to create an interactive dialogue system that functions according to a defined role and adapts to user characteristics in real-time. To achieve this, we have developed a system termed CHARACTERO, which is designed to generate responses that align with both user characteristics and system role, by fine-tuning large-scale models on parallel datasets created using natural language processing. Our experiments demonstrate that building role and user-specific dialogue by leveraging a scalable model outperforms alternative approaches, yielding more engaging and natural responses.

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbances known as the stochastic gravitational wave background. Researchers have found that this background has a unique signature, characterized by a specific frequency range, and is creating research opportunities for future detectors like LISA and its capacity to study the event rate of binary black hole mergers, particularly in the LIGO band and in space.

A hypothetical supersymmetry framework offers an explanation for why we only see one type of matter in the universe and how it formed, while also predicting significant disturbances during the early universe. These disturbances could create ripples detectable by future studies of space time fluctuations. In addition, these ripples are accompanied by heavy particles that act as the "seeds" for forming massive structures like black holes in space time. These heavy particles form through the fluctuations of the early universe, following a phase change that follows a second-order process. This theoretical model generates the necessary imbalance of matter, while predicting significant disturbances creating ripples in space time and large structures of dark matter.

A reliable and efficient communication system that goes beyond traditional semantics is needed to handle the growing data demands in real-world applications. A novel emergent semantic approach, grounded in a neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence model of cause and effect, is proposed to achieve this. A communication system that leverages this new causal reasoning model is designed as a signaling game to achieve causal understanding and generate efficient messages. Through the alignment of sender and receiver in terms of cause and effect, this game leads to a convergence on a cause-effect bridge that is a Nash equilibrium. For a simple control task, a complete understanding of the causal relationships is achieved, resulting in effective messages of length one token. For more complex control tasks, a partial understanding of the causal relationships leads to effective messages. This effective message concept is operationalized as the success rate of task completion, which is used to quantify the communication cost. Results show that the communication cost is significantly reduced with only 1 token for simple tasks and 10 tokens for more complex tasks, which significantly surpass a baseline model of 100 tokens.

The Natural Language Processing area has seen significant advancement in recent years, with word prediction being one of the most studied tasks.  A variety of methods have been proposed to address this problem, including statistical and neural network-based approaches.  The challenge lies in the need to account for the dependencies between words in a sentence within a limited context window, making it difficult to capture long-term relationships.  To overcome this limitation, a new hybrid model is presented that combines an n-gram model with a Bayesian information sharing approach.  The proposed model operates at the word level and is evaluated on the standard Williams & Yannai dataset, demonstrating improved performance over existing n-gram models.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained significant interest, outperforming traditional methods and providing personalized real-time suggestions. These models typically encode session history to identify user patterns, however, they often neglect the associated labels, leading to decreased accuracy. Recent models demonstrate improved results but are hindered by increased latency, rendering them impractical for real-time applications. Our proposed solution involves a new class of learnable candidate rank embeddings that enables efficient end-to-end training while maintaining high recommendation accuracy. Our model adopts a two-stage approach, initially selecting a subset of top-N items, and then choosing the most relevant one, effectively balancing accuracy and real-time performance. Our methodology also leverages the Markov property to forecast user behavior and utilizes batch training with noisy item sampling for efficient sebased embedding learning. Our experiments indicate superior performance over state-of-the-art systems, achieving a 20% reduction in ranking errors and a 70% reduction in latency. Our code is publicly available on the repository https://github.com/rohitkumar2001ce/care.

We examine a rigid molecule composed of multiple active particles, as it interacts with a surface while drifting along an activity gradient. Our research reveals that the center of a active molecule tends to orient against the activity gradient at low levels of interaction with the surface. To achieve a stable alignment with the molecule, we identify a narrow parameter space where the molecule exhibits tumbling alignment. Our findings further show that in certain areas of this parameter space, the molecule can transport itself against the activity gradient, and we propose that this effect can be used to develop active colloidal molecules that navigate against their preferred orientation.

A three-dimensional network of fractures is modeled within a continuous domain,
overlain by an extensive, porous matrix rock system. A discrete fracture-matrix
framework is implemented to simulate single-phase flow and solute transport.
This framework consists of distinct fracture and matrix blocks. We utilize a
mimetic finite difference (MFD) method, which enables the simulation of flow
within the fracture network. A set of linear equations is solved to determine
pressure in the fractures, and then a system of ordinary differential equations
describes how flow within the matrix blocks responds to changes in fracture
pressure. Our approach allows us to efficiently and accurately model this complex
system across an enormous range of scales.

This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of cellular automation for a drone swarm. Achieving and maintaining close-proximity formation flight is crucial for efficient flight across a number of applications, including the novel field of aerial photography. Traditionally, achieving and maintaining formation flight for a group of drones involves high energy collision avoidance, as well as difficult-to-implement control strategies due to the complex relative position and orientation relationships between each aircraft. These challenges can often be overcome through the use of a centralized control system, although this poses risks to flight safety in the absence of such a system. A more decentralized approach leverages the concept of geodesic distance and utilizes an energy-efficient, gradient descent-based collision avoidance strategy that translates and rotates each aircraft towards its target position, thereby effectively avoiding collisions at the level of individual flight. This method proves particularly effective when combined with a point set registration strategy based on the concept of a centroid, thereby facilitating the challenging formation flight collision avoidance problem in three-dimensional space.

This research focuses on determining lower bounds on the Seidel spectrum of a graph, while also of interest is the exact Seidel spectrum of chain graphs, which serves as an instance that achieves this bound. Additional investigation is conducted into the Energy of the Seidel matrix for semi-regular graphs, with a proposed conjecture of this energy being equal to $n$ in such cases. It is proven that for regular chain graphs, the energy of the Seidel matrix is strictly less than $n$, and some lower and upper bounds are established for the energy of the Seidel matrix in the case of bipartite semi-regular graphs.

In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which lacks sufficient randomness, we develop a control approach incorporating a novel driver and a novel white noise representation. This allows us to utilize standard optimal control techniques, which are based on It\u0027s decomposition and the Hida transform for converting fractional Brownian motion into white noise. This representation and decomposition enable us to derive explicit optimal solutions, which we then verify through a thorough mathematical analysis.

We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of non-self-adjoint Dirac operators with explicit, structured spectral properties. This structured spectrum includes discrete energy levels and continuous bands of spectra, with our specific operators having one continuous band of spectra. We've established a precise, comprehensive two-parameter set of these operators with spectra structured in multiple closed intervals, with a focus on operators having one continuous band of spectra with elliptic, smooth, and periodically repeating potential functions. For the class of operators with one continuous band of spectra, we've shown it has a non-degenerate, smooth, one-to-one correspondence with pairs of elliptic, smooth, anti-self-adjoint companion functions, preserving the form of a non-self-adjoint Dirac operator with periodic potential functions. Additionally, we've derived a unique, one-to-one correspondence between pairs of elliptic, smooth, anti-self-adjoint companion functions and other paired functions, related to our study of elliptic finite-band potentials of the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator.

RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating a wide range of applications,
but are often constrained in coverage and connectivity, particularly in areas
with high vehicle density. This study introduces a two-tier RSU-based vehicular
network, where vehicle relays bridge the gap to unconnected vehicles. We model the
network using a Markov chain, and derive the probability of successful packet
delivery and the route taken by packets to a specified RSU. We then develop
expressions for network metrics, including throughput and delay, taking into
account the vehicle's mobility. A key contribution of this study is the design
of an adaptive routing method where vehicle relays dynamically switch between
RSUs based on current traffic conditions, with the goal of maximizing overall
network throughput. Simulation results demonstrate that this adaptive approach
yields superior performance compared to a baseline method, where vehicle relays
are exclusively used.

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics. The encyclopedia continues to attract a large range of contributors who enhance over 400 million entries. Despite the vast amount of time they dedicate, the quality of their work varies significantly, making it challenging to evaluate without manual review by human editors. Maintaining high standards on the encyclopedia is crucial, as unwarranted deletion and increased effort are required to correct subpar content. To maintain the encyclopedia's integrity, we need to identify low-quality articles automatically, particularly those that have been recently modified, to pinpoint articles in need of in-depth evaluation. To achieve this, we have developed EditPatternMining, a system that utilizes machine learning to analyze patterns in editor behavior and automatically tag newly edited articles as low quality. By examining the impact of these associations on the encyclopedia, we can accurately identify these articles in real time. To maintain high standards on the encyclopedia, we need to understand and manage subpar content on Wikipedia.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a more complex, accurate model. Traditionally, this process involves copying the soft labels produced by the complex model, but this approach relies on the expensive, high-precision output of the target model. This new method uses a different approach by leveraging decision-based black-box query attacks to guide the training of the complex model, thereby avoiding the need for its high-precision output. This approach is more efficient and effective, as it relies on a different type of output from the target model, which is easier to compute.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7, 8, and 14 TeV by the LHCb experiment at CERN. The measured branching fractions are $3.04^{+0.59}_{-0.49}\times10^{-4}$ and $1.4^{+0.6}_{-0.5}\times10^{-4}$, respectively. Moreover, the ratio of these decay rates, $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ to $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0
K^0_S$, has been calculated as $0.47^{+0.24}_{-0.19}$, and the corresponding masses and transition form factors have been determined or compared to prior studies, with several results showing good agreement with earlier findings.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality is utilized to establish a
more robust version of standard T-duality for twisted tori, adhering to the
principles of Morita equivalence, which is a foundational concept in our theory.
To accomplish this, we examine the K-theory of twisted tori through two distinct yet
equivalent methodologies: one leveraging equivariant $K$-theory and the other
exploiting a specific class of projective representations, termed twisted Hilbert
$C^*$-algebras. To facilitate our analysis, we also incorporate an in-depth discussion
of twisted tori, lexicographic basis systems, and twisted coefficients, which may
have broader implications in noncommutative topology. To illustrate our approach,
we apply it to simplified examples, such as the circle, a torus, and a twisted torus
in a lower dimension.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly improved through imitation learning, which learns from expert examples. A challenge arises when there are no direct expert demonstrations available. To address this, CoImation is introduced, a novel co-training approach that improves both imitation and reinforcement learning. CoImation's two sub-tasks involve learning from indirect expert knowledge (behavioral policy) through behavioral augmentation, and enhancing agents with complementary skills for better generalizability. Evaluations of CoImation's performance are conducted on simple reconfiguration and complex manipulation tasks within an actual robotic environment. Results indicate that CoImation achieves superior policy generalization and robustness compared to traditional reinforcement learning methods learned solely through direct expert demonstration.

This paper proposes a novel metric for assessing the performance of Prefix-free Arithmetic Compression (PAC) codes, and proves that this metric precisely quantifies the compression efficiency of any PAC code. Building on this metric, we derive universal arithmetic compression methods that achieve optimal performance according to this new standard. To do so, we devise novel approaches for both time and resource management during the arithmetic compression process, which may have broader applications in data transformation.

This project focuses on tracking hands within scenes, predicting hand poses, and reconstructing scene geometry from sequential point cloud data, all of which are essential challenges in visual tracking and hand pose estimation. Traditionally, hand tracking and scene reconstruction have been approached separately, while predicting hand poses within 3D environments remains an unsolved problem. Our work tackles these difficulties by leveraging sequential point cloud data, which provides valuable information for tracking hands within scenes. Our method employs a data-driven hand predictor enhanced with optical flow-based data, combined with a triangular mesh-based scene builder that simultaneously predicts hand poses and scene geometry. Notably, our system doesn't require any manual annotations or pre-existing models, and performs hand tracking and scene tracking in real-time. Our evaluation shows that our system surpasses current state-of-the-art models in various benchmarks.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

A novel, markerless robot-depth camera calibration and end-effector pose estimation system is introduced, utilizing depth data from a robot's Depth First Sensor to eliminate the need for visual markers. A learning-based approach is employed to develop a novel robot-depth camera calibration and pose estimation method, which was tested on a robot featuring a customized end-effector with two distinct shapes. Our proposed method eliminates the need for external cameras, simplifying setup and reducing expenses, and overcomes the constraints of traditional, marker-based methods.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced by its neighboring units. A multiple regression 
framework is proposed that enables a comprehensive analysis of unit responses 
and facilitates complete inference about treatment effects, potentially 
utilizing local time series data as input as well. To ensure reliable results, 
a novel identification assumption is developed that treats neighbors as randomly 
selected from a larger pool of units. A statistical test is created to evaluate 
this assumption's validity and a step-wise procedure is designed to confirm 
its fulfillment before proceeding with result interpretation. Moreover, 
simulations are conducted to demonstrate the reliability of our approach in 
meeting nominal error rates and showing competitive power over existing 
methods in treating treatment effects.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from positron-electron annihilation in neutron star cores, assuming a pseudoscalar interaction with Dark Matter, have been conducted. Given the core's electron fermion density is chiral, it can couple to such an interaction, enabling the process of annihilation into two neutrinos. Since the core temperature is lower than the neutrino decay energy, it results in enhanced emissions. With the core's Density is higher than a lab setting, this leads to significantly increased neutrino emissions compared to the standard model. These findings may be utilized to refine constraints on such interactions through neutron star observations.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has finished its data collection using the Magellan/Baade telescope and the Magellan/Broadband Optical Imaging spectrograph. To complement the main survey, the Magellan/Baadow Optical Imaging Spectrograph has taken deep images of 15 fields in the sky, allowing for a study of cosmic structure. To analyze these images, a new pipeline called ShapePipe was created, which measures the shape of galaxies more accurately than previous methods, resulting in better estimates of the power spectrum and false spectra rates. When analyzing the lensing effects of the light from galaxies, it was found that there are some systematic errors in the data that need to be taken into account. Although the current results are not suitable to be used on their own to study the lensing effects, they provide enough information to understand how to correct these errors in the future.

A notable result from Koksma in 1936 demonstrated that taking modulo 1 within a linear combination of logarithms of irrational numbers leads to a uniform distribution. Building upon Koksma's foundational work, a specific variant result involving the fractional parts of the negative half squares of linear combinations of these logarithms was proved in a specific paper, which relied on diophantine approximation methods akin to Hamel's. In contrast, another paper that used a geometric-based approach led to a different formulation of the same result, which relied on the evenness of the quadratic function used in the fractional part. These two results prompted a new inquiry into the general applicability of the geometric approach to Weyl type theorems, which was answered in a subsequent paper that offered a broader definition of the notion of evenness for multivariate functions, which enabled a broader class of theorems that hold for logarithmic mappings and other functions, which are generated by continuous, bounded, even, and locally Lipschitz functions in a specific, positive definite quadratic form, which are nonnegative. This new theorem generalizes prior work by Hamel, Jarn\'ik, and Zeckendorf and provides a broader understanding of the half-square fractional part phenomenon.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local complete intersections related to Fermi singularities are shown to be non-k-rational.

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a 3D spin-1/2 Heisenberg model using a neutron resonance in an imperfect Heisenberg antiferromagnet. When a magnetic field is applied to the compound $(Ba_{0.95}La_{0.05})MnO_3$, it initially behaves as a 3D Heisenberg model until it reaches a two-dimensional single-layer structure. Through experimental measurements and theoretical simulations, it is demonstrated that the system exhibits field-induced two-dimensional behavior for low-energy spin excitations, even within its 3D single-layer structure. Analyzing these results, it is established that field-induced two-dimensional behavior is driven by the exchange of a specific type of spin excitation, known as transverse magnons, and is supported by the presence of a field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless phase transition, as evidenced by the temperature variation of spin expectation. This is the first time such phenomena have been observed in a 3Heisenberg model, which is a fundamental model used to understand spin interactions in quantum systems.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion to the standard model creates a system that naturally contains both dark matter and dark energy. This model features an unstable, highly-massive dark sector that interacts with standard model particles. A combination of axion and sterile neutrino dark matter is consistent with multiple phenomena, including X-ray emissions, baryon abundance, and structure development. A related modification to the seesaw mechanism prevents excessively heavy Majorana neutrinos from being produced by colliding neutrinos, thus avoiding conflicts with axion-based dark matter theories. This theoretical framework predicts new particles that are potentially detectable through axion searches, nebular observations, and analyses of the cosmic background.

This study enhances the known limit on how rapidly certain unitary circuits can increase the stabilizer rank of specific quantum states when decomposed into simpler components. The focus is on a key state, often referred to as the T-state, which is crucial for universal quantum computation, and its relative efficiency is measured in terms of its ability to break down into simpler parts. The research raises an important question about whether there's a linear relationship between the size of such decompositions and the number of qubits in the state, and currently, the best answer is a quadratic one. The team makes significant progress by improving the exponent of this quadratic relationship, moving it closer to being linear, and achieving a new record of approximately 0.66. The research also considers more general scenarios and provides a clearer understanding of how to calculate the rank of specific subsets of these decompositions, and even shows that in some cases, the rank of these subsets can be linearly related to the number of qubits. The new method used in this research involves creating novel state subsets that are nearly independent of one another, and are ultimately shown to be instances of the original decompositions, and are known as relative projections. The research provides a general framework for analyzing the rank of these subsets, and demonstrates their potential to yield new insights into the quantum computational process.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, with a particular focus on non-interacting scenarios.
Assisting in the analysis is a modified quintessence model based on complex scalar fields,
which facilitates an in-depth examination of the model from theoretical and cosmological aspects.
The study examines various statefinder, dimensionless diagnostic, and Hessian analysis 
for the derived scale factor solutions, evaluated using the beltran law for complex scalar fields.
The findings indicate that this model from the Tsallis approach is preferable to other approaches, 
such as Ray-Singer or Gauss-Bonnet, in the Tsallis approach for explaining the acceleration of the universe.
In addition, the complex scalar field in the Quintessence model allows us to determine a mass 
for the scalar field, which corresponds to a hypothetical mass for the dark energy carrier.
The study also presents a phase diagram for the evolution of the dark energy density and 
the work density of the fluid from the derived potential.

Between October 2019 and January 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observation, using 4000 individual fields with 4000 individual objects in each field, resulting in a vast amount of highly connected spectral data for approximately 11 million objects across the sky. The LAMOST Time-Domain Survey (LTS), a vital component of the LAMOST DR8 release, encompasses 90% of the sky and consists of approximately 2.6 trillion individual spectral records, with three additional datasets integrated into the survey data. The first results based on four LAMOST plates reveal that the average spectral measurement accuracy is 3.58, with a notable detection of 206 astrophysically significant variable stars. The LTS survey data has the potential to provide valuable insights into various areas of study, such as categorizing variable stars, analyzing the properties of galaxies, tracking the movement of stars, and monitoring rapid changing celestial objects. The LTS survey will greatly contribute to our understanding of the universe, with the full dataset expected to significantly advance our knowledge in these areas in the future.

Recent years have seen a growing interest in SRAM-based TRNGs, but issues with supply voltage quality often hinder their effectiveness. To overcome these problems, supply voltage scaling is typically employed to enhance the probability mass function's uniformity. Nevertheless, this supply underscaling method has not been thoroughly analyzed for its impact and efficiency, resulting in a compromise between performance and TRNG output quality. To overcome this dilemma, a novel approach, TuRaN, is proposed, which utilizes supply voltage underscaling only in particular parts of the SRAM, thus offering improved design flexibility and efficiency. Through thorough simulations, TuRaN's performance was evaluated, demonstrating an optimal balance between efficiency and output quality, with the supply underscaling rate and the probability of selecting a seed from the partial region being key variables.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been
conducted, incorporating a particular molecule, where electron transport is regulated
by a combination of tunnel barrier transistors and a molecular resistive switch. 
Two terminal attachments to the molecule were considered: a carbon atom in the molecule's
outer ring and a more positively charged atom located near the molecule's center. 
Initial research was carried out on the switch transistors to determine their optimal
parameters, focusing in particular on a tunnel barrier formed between two gold atoms.
Following this, simulations of electron transport through the molecule were conducted
under an applied voltage. It was discovered that for the atom with a carbon structure,
the molecule exhibits a positive resistance, while a resistive switch behavior is observed
for the atom with the more positively charged state. Notably, this switch exhibits a
significant change in current of over three orders of magnitude, along with a substantial
energy barrier separating the resistive and conductive states. Furthermore, the molecule
exhibits a substantial Coulomb blockade and, using a theoretical model, it has been
estimated that the tunnel transit times are substantially shorter than the electron lifetime
within the molecule's central atomic site.

We introduce an alternative approach to the numerical solution of multi-loop Feynman integrals, built on the concept of topological amplitude and the all-scale representation. This approach is based on a systematic algorithm for the topological expansion of polylog functions, enabling the evaluation of multi-loop diagrams with any topology across all scales. Unlike traditional methods, our approach circumvents the complications of branch cuts in complex functions. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we apply the method to the precise numerical calculation of the hadronic $\pi^+\pi^-\to K^+K^-$ elastic scattering cross-section up to two-loop order, yielding highly accurate next-to-next-to-leading order QCD predictions for various kinematic quantities in $\gamma^* \to$ hadrons decay processes, including elastic scattering form factors, annihilation form form factors, and radium form forms.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A set of two functions is used to derive the unique measure from the resolvent kernel, which in turn yields the eigenfunction expansion formula. Moreover, a crucial result is proved, stating that under specific conditions, this measure is non-negative, thereby ensuring the convergence of a convergent eigenfunction expansion. A simple quantum model serves as a demonstration of the application of the derived theory, giving rise to closed-form expressions for the resolvent kernel and a unique measure, along with the corresponding eigenfunction expansion.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems offers a unique opportunity to delve into the non-Bose statistics of photons and phonons and the non-Hermitian nature of interactions, thereby raising important questions about the consequences of q-deformation on Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) of optomechanical components. To address these queries, our investigation centers on the impact of q-deformation on optical transparency, delay, and fast light within linear and nonlinear optomechanical systems, with particular emphasis on the occurrence of BEC. As expected, our study reveals that the optimal q-deformation value for inducing optical transparency, delay, and fast light is near zero, whereas q-deformation value greater than zero facilitates optical reflection, anti-delay, and anti-fast light. Moreover, our work showcases how q-deformation value affects both phonon and photon emission rates and, intriguingly, determines whether BEC occurs in such systems.

In a previous study, I developed a model for the two-rotors system with negative scissors states, excluding those with R-parity conservation, and found that this model accurately described negative scissors states in $^{166}$Er and $^{168}$Er. This time, I include R-parity conservation and apply the model to study and predict negative scissors states in even-even nuclei of Er and Yb isotopes. I investigated how the inter-irreducible space coupling constant affects the results and compared my calculation outcomes with available experimental data for Er and Yb isotopes.

The properties of thin films made of transition-metal oxides can be controlled through the application of dimensional constraints, which significantly alter their electronic behavior compared to their bulk counterparts. This manipulation gives rise to novel states that have far-reaching applications in superconductivity and spintronics. In our research carried out at ultrathin barium titanate and strontium titanate films grown on lanthanum aluminate, we applied spin-orbit and exchange interactions, which modulate the electronic state. This application led to evidence of orbital and spin fluctuations, which were detected using in situ x-ray scattering and Raman scattering. Ultimately, our findings can help to predict and explore new phases in oxide materials.

The occurrence of diffusion, both normal and anomalous, is a common phenomenon in nature. In the context of laser cooling, atoms in equilibrium typically follow a normal distribution, but when this equilibrium is disrupted, atoms may enter a non-stationary state, potentially exhibiting anomalous distribution characteristics. We investigate the distribution dynamics of laser-cooled atoms in an optical lattice within a far-red Doppler cooling regime, where cooling rates are much lower than the lattice's fundamental frequency, using a combination of master equation and numerical simulations. The simulation reveals that when the laser detuning and diffusion become intertwined, the distribution of atoms in the lattice becomes non-intuitive, with atoms trapped in the lattice exhibiting an allocation pattern that deviates from standard norms, becoming more pronounced as cooling slows and the diffusion rate decreases. This effect is particularly noticeable in the case of trapped atoms, whose behavior mimics that of a lattice of quantum spins in a magnetic field, resulting in a "blocked" allocation pattern in which no two atoms occupy adjacent lattice sites. Additionally, we explore the dynamics of atoms in the lattice that undergo a diffusion transition and observe an over-shooting phenomenon in which the distribution dynamics of atoms occasionally exceed their normal limits in a way that resembles a lattice of quantum spins with flipped orientation in comparison to the blocked case.

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets. Firstly, a cryptocurrency trading network is defined by employing cryptocurrencies as nodes and weekly log returns on a given exchange as edges. Pairwise correlations are examined, revealing low levels of correlation and weak impacts, with notable increases in correlation observed during the coronavirus pandemic. Cross-correlation analysis shows a predominant unidirectional flow of information from Bitcoin to altcoins. Furthermore, a network-based approach called spectral analysis is introduced, revealing intricate higher-order interactions. Results show that a significant portion of cryptocurrency market's power spectrum can be explained by these networks, with low levels of interaction in normal conditions and increased interaction during the pandemic. Spectral analysis also identifies a strong two-way relationship between Bitcoin and Ethereum. Finally, a network model is proposed, defining a complexity parameter that quantifies the magnitude of fluctuations. Findings indicate that the magnitude of fluctuations is influenced by the network position, with central nodes exhibiting less volatility than peripheral ones.

The formation of new particles by converting sulfuric acid into a new phase is a crucial process in the cloud formation layer high in the atmosphere, and its rate is largely influenced by particles' zero-point vibrational movements, particularly in the transition from gas to solid. To better understand this phenomenon in a basic model, a molecular dynamics simulation was conducted using a quantum approach to calculate zero-point movements in small clusters of sulfuric acid and water before and after they transition to a crystalline structure. These movements were determined by making adjustments to the nuclear path integral method in the simulation, which revealed that movements at extremely low temperatures significantly affect the bacterial acid component's probability of being found near the center, thus impacting its tendency to condense into a solid. These movements significantly affect the bacterial acid component's probability of being found near the center, thus impacting its tendency to condense into a solid. In contrast, water molecules exhibit minimal changes in their positional vibrations within the cluster.

We establish the definition of a compactification for a perception pair (X,Q), employing a compact set (C,d_C) with a canonical map (f:C|_Q=f^*(f:C)) :X-> c, which preserves the structure of (X,Q). It is required that (f :X-> C)circ(q:x-> x[q])=q :C-> c, where (x-> x[q]) denotes the quantization map, a continuous function from Q to C. Additionally, we derive the canonical action extension of homeomorphisms C as well as the continuous boundary system homeomorphisms C, which cover a wide range of compactifications, characterizing all perception pair compactifications, and allow for a compactification of a perception pair (X,Q) under specific conditions. Furthermore, we define the space of homeomorphisms on (X,d), which are equivariant under action of a group G, and have the property of being non-expansive under the metric d, denoted as [G,Homeo_{G}(X,d)]^{d}, and prove that it is a compact, path-connected, and locally path-connected compactification under the condition of action continuity and existence of vanishing ideal under certain conditions. Lastly, we obtain a compactification of a perception pair (X,Q) under the condition that (Q,d_Q) is bounded under the condition of existence and continuity of homeomorphisms on (Q,d_Q) and

The way solids respond to temperature gradients is an area with limited understanding. The transport properties of quantum liquids have been theoretically linked to the effects of gravito-thermal forces through an analogy, but this comparison lacks an experimental basis until now. By measuring the Hall response in Ising ferromagnets, we found that this response cannot be explained by a gravitational analogy, and we mathematically established that this very Hall effect must exist. Our research shows that the Hall conductance is directly related to the energy current correlations, confirming an assumption that has been made to infer thermal properties. Furthermore, we found that the Hall response is sensitive to the chiral edge modes present in these systems and may serve as an effective tool to study these edge modes.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, architecture design, and training techniques, each with unique outcomes. By using a family of neural network models with parameterized geometric complexity measures, we determine their stochastic training dynamics, examine how different training and design factors influence the model's complexity, and explore the relationship between model complexity, inductive biases, and performance. Our analysis reveals that simpler models exhibit strong, parameter-free relationships with their complexity, and we create a framework that can predict the model's behavior based on its complexity, which also helps explain phenomena such as the over-smoothing in graph neural networks, the "no free lunch" issue in learning tasks, and the performance drop in deep learning models.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay scoring using machine learning is a well-established approach, 
but building robust models requires extensive, balanced datasets that are 
often impractical to create from scratch. To overcome this limitation, 
augmented datasets are being developed by introducing data enhancement 
techniques that improve the model's performance. This study explores the 
effectiveness of three data augmentation techniques on automated essay 
scoring and the influence of sequence length on the performance of 
Transformer-based language models. The results show that augmented datasets 
yield improved models, with specific transformations such as delete, random 
synonym, and dropout proving most effective. Additionally, training 
transformer models on student-generated essays is feasible, and the 
performance of these models approaches that of human-generated data.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques and establish a database for small model examples.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can be viewed as dynamic platforms that need to be assigned to different age groups within a mobility framework. Our study addresses this by determining how to dynamically and equitably distribute opportunities across different age groups, taking into account the mobility patterns within each group. Our model reveals the trade-offs between social fairness and economic efficiency. Our findings demonstrate that, in order to achieve the highest level of equity and efficiency, individuals and societies need to make decisions based on their position in different probability distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our allocation strategy can help individuals and societies navigate the complexity of intergenerational mobility, ensuring that opportunities are distributed in a way that prioritizes their potential to move people out of different social strata.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports multi-signature public keys, which is essential for dynamic, anonymous networks like blockchain. This advancement enables the creation of delegated RingCT signatures, offering a 10x performance boost over traditional RingCT while substantially shrinking signature and public key sizes. Additionally, we've developed an efficient method to verify these signatures by leveraging a novel property of Bulletproofs, resulting in enhanced verification efficiency.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the first detection of three massive gauge bosons being produced simultaneously in high-energy collisions of protons, as predicted by the Standard Model. These collisions were conducted at the CERN LHC with the CMS detector, using 13 TeV of energy. The study involved scrutinizing events containing either three leptons or seven stable particles resulting from the collisions. The detected number of events matched the predicted outcomes, and the study also included an examination of the differences between various boson combinations. Notably, the analysis focused on the potential of distinguishing between different types of boson production based on kinematic characteristics.

We have undertaken UD-style parsing of diverse text sources, including religious, news, and online text, using a pre-trained word embedding model. Initially, we employed the Hebrew-SPAR project's conditional random field (CRF) parser, which, after tuning, achieved a 84.77 UAS score on the Hebrew-SPAR training set. Subsequently, we incorporated pre-trained word embeddings into the CRF model, boosting the accuracy to 87.43 UAS. This level of performance placed the model second in a competition, where it demonstrated adaptability to unseen test sets. By leveraging pre-trained word embeddings, we were able to improve parsing performance without needing extensively annotated training data, allowing us to efficiently train the model on a corpus that was only sparsely annotated. Furthermore, our results show that adding word embeddings can enhance the CRF-based parser's performance on the MWTI-MHEP creational patterns detection task.

We have created a method for reducing the dimension of vectors while maintaining their distances with a factor of $\epsilon$, which also works well for subsets of incompressible data when using the $L_p$ space with parameters where $1 \le p \le 2$. This method significantly lowers the dimension by a factor of four compared to previous methods, achieving an even better result for subsets where the Johnson-Schechtmann theorem can be applied. Furthermore, we believe this dimension reduction technique is the best possible given its applications in lossy data compression.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial intelligence, specifically deep learning, have transformed our understanding of multiple scientific and engineering disciplines by enabling accurate material property predictions from large datasets.  Computational scientists are now applying these advancements to further research, but isolated efforts in the AI material community fail to capture the growing trend towards collaboration and knowledge sharing.  To address this gap, we introduce the concept of cooperative AI modeling and propose a framework to facilitate this modeling type.  The framework emphasizes two essential components: standardization and transparency.  We also develop a systematic cooperative learning protocol to enable and support this modeling.  By doing so, we aim to increase efficiency, reduce redundancy, maximize resource utilization, accelerate research progress, and build a reliable knowledge base for scientific and engineering endeavors.

Current studies have revealed that degree-degree correlation in low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes significantly impacts their performance. We investigate the erasure decoding behavior of d-biased binary LDPC ensembles in the large block size limit. Our findings confirm that degree-degree correlation in ensembles can be modeled using a bipartite sparse random graph. We derive the asymptotic stopping threshold for d-biased binary ensemble with correlation degree and significantly. This outcome indicates that to enhance the stopping threshold, degree-degree correlation should assign higher degrees to variable nodes. Our results also demonstrate that for a specified stopping threshold, there is an optimal correlation that yields the maximum average degree degree among all ensembles. This optimal correlation assigns greater degrees to variable nodes than to check nodes. Our analysis also shows that ensembles with negative correlation exhibit lower stopping thresholds than those with no correlation. Our study also reveals a link between the average degree and the spectral stopping threshold of ensemble with correlation degree, and confirms that the spectral threshold is lower than the iterative threshold for all ensembles with correlation.

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances, especially in complex systems with non-linear dynamics and complex constraints. Current methods, which are based on control barrier functions, can handle linear and concave constraints but struggle with systems having complex or non-convex constraints. To overcome this limitation, a new safety filter, which is based on system-level synthesis, has been introduced. This novel filter, which is efficient in computational terms, can handle a broader range of systems and constraints by integrating system models and incorporating future references. Experimental results, which were conducted on a cart-pole system and an aerial vehicle, have demonstrated the effectiveness of this safety filter.

A critical flaw exists in the current implementation of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems that makes them vulnerable to the time-resolved multi-photon attack (TRMPA). In an effort to counter such attacks, the present work proposes two novel anti-TRMPA measures which can be implemented using existing hardware. One such method involves accurately measuring the probability of emitting multi-photon pulses from the QKD system's source, thereby accurately calculating and subtracting the associated key rates in the post-processing phase. In order to counter TRMPA in scenarios where the source's multi-photon emission probability is unknown, the present work has developed a security bound based on the real-world behavior of the QKD system's beam splitter under the assumption of low-rate lattice attack (LLA). By analyzing a data set generated under the belief that specific probabilities are assigned to different bases and decoding methods, the security bound can be calculated using the next-time random number that the lattice attack would yield in the most favorable circumstance. Notably, this new bound holds true even in the event of incomplete phase randomization as long as the probability of emitting single photons does not exceed multi-photon emissions by more than 10%.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context learning, where models can perform well on various tasks with minimal fine-tuning. Our research investigates the influence of large, pretraining corpora on a model's in-context learning capabilities. We find that models with extensive pretraining exposure not only learn tasks more quickly and achieve higher accuracy, but also learn to generate text that is more coherent, fluent, and semantically relevant. Our findings have implications for models' ability to learn tasks without extensive training, such as in the fields of search, information retrieval, and search. Additionally, our analysis reveals that both the content and linguistic structure of pretraining data contribute to a model's in-context learning performance. Our results are discussed in light of recent theoretical and theoretical work on language models' latent representations, suggesting that large, pretraining corpora enable models to perform tasks more effectively both with and without the aid of contextual information.

Galaxy cluster observations reveal an unexpected low field strength and temperature ratio, suggesting a possible initial cold component that hasn't fully incorporated into the present hot environment. To investigate this theory, we used a numerical simulation to model the development of early, cooling fields and compared the results to real-world observations. Our findings indicate that the present hot environment's low field and temperature ratio could be explained by fields that initially formed, supporting the hypothesis of a primordial field. However, the fields we found didn't completely support the theory of a cold field, implying other fields, such as a primordially magnetic field, could also explain shattering and seed the turbulence we see today.
The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty and charm is summarised, incorporating insights gained from the latest LHCb results presented at the conference.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their counterparts in bosonic string theory are significantly weaker. A remarkable relationship exists among these amplitudes, where one is proportional to the others, proportional to their respective polarization components. Calculations of their high-energy limits and polarization-decomposed versions have also been determined. Additionally, it has been found that this amplitude is connected to a specific high-energy limit of a bosonic string scattering amplitude. This connection validates the Gross proposal for superstring scattering amplitudes.

To effectively manage the growing number of 5G small cells, new strategies are required to handle their unique challenges, including dynamic workload variations, energy consumption, and fault management. To address these complexities, the concept of self-organizing and sustainable 5G small cell networks has been developed, which incorporates novel management procedures to optimize performance, including automated configuration, configuration adjustment, real-time monitoring, fault detection, prevention, recovery, evaluation, and energy-efficient operation. This paper explores the novel management procedures needed to configure and sustain 5G small cell networks, presenting a comprehensive framework for managing these networks in a cost-effective, reliable, and scalable manner.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a universal communication tool for individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing by enabling them to comprehend spoken language through text. Text-based speech synthesis has limitations in accurately representing and reproducing the acoustic details of phoneme durations and spectral characteristics. As a result, produced speech may be of low quality or even unintelligible. This research introduces a novel text-to-speech synthesis approach based on the analysis of spoken words without requiring speech examples. Our method is based on a data structure called perceptual acoustic units (PAUs), which are used to organize the storage and computation of acoustic details for any arbitrary text. Each unit within a PAU represents a segment of a word, and is associated with the start time, end time, and phoneme it corresponds to. Each PAU is defined by three characteristics: the type of acoustic unit, text-based features, and speech features. Since not all PAUs can be identified for a given word due to varying acoustic details, PaUZOR fills in these gaps using an optimization technique that takes into consideration start and end times, and other relevant features. Moreover, a PaUZOR-based speech synthesis system with the capability to perform accurate speech synthesis with pauzor features and a text-to-speech synthesis method that can perform the desired action.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging non-convex optimization problem. Using a multi-stage approach, we develop a significant algorithm that incorporates data-driven McCormick envelope relaxations to improve the efficiency of pos-vel optimization. Across various test cases, our method shows a marked improvement over standard methods, reducing runtime by as much as a factor of 17 and achieving zero optimality gap in many cases.

We have developed a family of constraints that apply to all stochastic maps in order to determine if two quantum states are transformable into one another. This stochastic map includes both quantum channels and classical probability distributions.
